Sustainability Leadership RetreatWorking draft · September 2026

A retreat for people doing sustainability work

A few days outside,
with people who
do this work.

Two nights away. Time to know each other properly, reconnect with what brings out our best, and work through something real.

Come back with people you can call when the work gets hard.

A small group. Different organizations.
Enough in common to understand.
Two nights outside12–18 participants proposedFall 2026 or spring 2027Within reach of New York City
The vision

A peer circle that begins here.

This retreat brings together early and mid-career sustainability professionals working from different seats: companies, financial institutions, nonprofits, public agencies, and advisory firms. People with enough experience to have hit the hard parts, and enough runway that how they handle them still shapes their path.

We want to begin a circle of peers who help one another stay effective and find a sustainable way to do this work. People with whom you can be candid, ask for help, and recover perspective.

That is a lot to ask of two nights. The weekend can start the relationships, make room for reflection, and give each person practice on one live challenge. What happens afterward will determine whether the group becomes a place to return to.

What we hope you leave with

A few people who know you better. A clearer sense of what drives your best work. One hard conversation you feel more ready to have.

Why now

The work asks a lot of us.

The mandate shifts with the politics. The budget gets cut and the goal stays. You are asked to move people who do not report to you, inside organizations that were not built for the problem you were hired to solve.

Many of us do that work with a thin bench of peers who understand it, and little time to step back. We need room to talk about what has been hard, notice what is working, and help each other navigate what comes next.

01

Know each other.

Shared meals, paired walks, and conversations that go well beyond the professional introduction.

02

Notice what drives us.

Reflect on when we do our best work, what makes it possible, and what pulls us away from it.

03

Practice something real.

Bring one challenge involving conflict or influence. Rehearse a conversation and hear what others see.

Why outside

Let the setting do some of the work.

Setting up camp and cooking together gives everyone a part in making the weekend happen. Walking makes some conversations easier. And for people whose work concerns the natural world, there is value in spending two nights in it.

We will leave laptops behind and make space for quiet, wandering, long meals, and unplanned conversations. There is no obligation to fill every hour.

Expect tents, sleeping bags, camp cooking, and shared facilities. Some of the places we are considering also have cabins. We will share a gear list and help with kit. No camping experience is required; the activities and arrangements will be clear before you commit.

Sessions can happen outdoors. An indoor meeting room is optional; the site and weather will shape the rhythm.

The shape of the weekend

Enough structure.
Room to breathe.

Two central pieces of work: understanding what brings out our best, and practicing one difficult conversation. Around them, time outside and time with one another.

A proposed Friday-to-Sunday rhythm. Times will flex around trains, campsite check-in and check-out, weather, and the needs of the group.

01

Friday

Arrive and land.

Get comfortable in the place, and with the people.

  1. 12–3 p.m.

    Travel, arrive, set up.

    Travel together where possible. Set up camp, find the water and facilities, and help everyone get settled before the afternoon begins.

  2. 3–3:30 p.m.

    A walk in pairs.

    What has been taking up your attention lately? What would make these few days useful?

  3. 3:30–5 p.m.

    The first circle.

    How you came into this work, a moment that made it real, and something you are carrying now. Agree how we will listen, respect the choice to pass, and keep personal stories within the group.

  4. 5–6:30 p.m.

    Cook together.

    Small teams take responsibility for food, water, and getting dinner ready. Everyone has a part.

  5. 6:30 p.m.

    Dinner.

    A shared meal, with time to linger and clean up together.

  6. 8 p.m. onward

    Optional fireside on careers.

    An open conversation around the fire about turning points: a decision that changed your path, a compromise you now see differently, how your definition of useful work has changed. Join, listen, or turn in early.

02

Saturday

What brings out
our best?

Some reflection. One practical skills lab. A long pause between them.

  1. 7:30 a.m.

    Coffee, quiet, optional movement.

    Ease into the day at your own pace.

  2. 8:30 a.m.

    Breakfast.

    Shared, simple, unhurried.

  3. 9:30–11 a.m.

    When I am at my best.

    Reflect on two real moments: one when you were doing your best work and one when you were struggling. Through time alone and conversation, look at the values, relationships, conditions, and choices that made the difference.

  4. 11–11:15 a.m.

    Take a break.

    Coffee, a stretch, a little space.

  5. 11:15 a.m.–noon

    What do others notice?

    In small groups, tell one of those stories and hear what peers see. Leave with a clearer account of what you need to do your best work and what tends to pull you away from it.

  6. 12–4:30 p.m.

    Hike and talk: the conversation you need to have.

    Head out on the trail in groups of three with packed lunches. Each person brings one live challenge involving conflict or influence. Take turns as the person working the case, the other party, and an observer. Consider what each person may be trying to protect. Rehearse, get specific feedback, and try again. Stop for lunch whenever your three decide.

  7. 4:30–5 p.m.

    A pause.

    Set the work down before the evening.

  8. 5–6:30 p.m.

    Cook together.

    Change teams, make dinner, and let the conversations find their own direction.

  9. 6:30 p.m.

    Dinner.

    Eat well, linger, and clean up together.

  10. 8 p.m. onward

    Free time.

    A fire if conditions allow. Stories, games, quiet, or sleep.

03

Sunday

What will we
take with us?

Ask for help. Offer something. Make a plan to meet again.

  1. 7:30 a.m.

    Coffee and quiet.

    One more morning outside.

  2. 8:30–10 a.m.

    Breakfast and pack up.

    Eat, take down tents, and organize shared gear. Move to a day-use area if the campsite requires an early check-out.

  3. 10–11:15 a.m.

    A circle we can use.

    Return to yesterday’s practice: what is clearer, what is still difficult, and what help would be useful? Each person makes a concrete ask and offers something to the group.

  4. 11:15 a.m.–noon

    Close together.

    One thing you understand differently, one move you want to make, and someone you will check in with. Agree how we will stay connected.

  5. 12–1 p.m.

    Lunch, final clean-up, depart.

    Leave time for station transfers and the journey home.

After we get home

Give the relationships somewhere to go.

Before leaving, choose a peer partner or group of three for a check-in within a month. We propose one facilitated reunion around six weeks later: what you tried, what happened, and where you need the group now. From there, we decide together what is useful.

Five possibilities

Somewhere
we can settle in.

Camping, water, trails, and room to be together. We are prioritizing a group camp in the woods, with an easy way onto the trails. An indoor meeting room is optional.

Park locations for orientation, not confirmed camp entrances. Open the selected place in Google Maps ↗

Harriman State Park · Pioneer group camping

Cedar Pond

One camp for the group, with forest all around.

The strongest new lead for a simple shared camp. Cedar Pond has three group sites by Lake Tiorati, with access to Harriman’s extensive trail network. A group site could let us cook, gather, and sleep in one place.

Getting there
Train from Penn via Secaucus to Harriman, then a pre-booked taxi. Allow roughly 2–2½ hours as a first planning estimate; confirm the correct camp entrance and transfer before choosing trains.
Staying together
Up to 30 people per site. Running water and pit toilets; no electricity or on-site showers. The published site fee is $37.50 a night, excluding all other retreat costs.
Timing
The published season runs from the third Friday in April through Columbus Day. Minimum two nights, or three over a holiday weekend. Beach showers are seasonal and should not be assumed for a fall retreat.
To work through
Applications require a bona fide organization. Confirm that this facilitated adult retreat qualifies, the available dates, and any gathering or cooking restrictions with the Lake Tiorati office.
Group camping details and application ↗

Harriman State Park · Appalachian Mountain Club

AMC Harriman Center

A pond in the woods, with a few things taken care of.

The Stephen & Betsy Corman Outdoor Center combines tent platforms and rustic cabins with shared facilities, trails, and access to Breakneck Pond.

Getting there
Train from Penn via Secaucus to Sloatsburg, then the AMC shuttle. Plan roughly 1½–2 hours on a coordinated connection. The shuttle requires advance booking.
Staying together
Platforms, shelters, or cabins, plus showers and optional meals. Ask about a group block and how we can keep shared cooking in the weekend.
Timing
The published 2026 season runs through October 18. Spring 2027 dates will need confirmation with AMC.
To work through
Shuttle capacity for the group, the mix of tents and cabins, and sharing common spaces with other guests. Indoor space is available if useful.
Explore AMC Harriman ↗

Hudson Highlands · New York State Park

Fahnestock

A woodland retreat with plenty of room to walk.

The group wilderness campground is worth a closer look. Fahnestock offers a substantial trail network, including the Appalachian Trail, within reach of the Hudson Line.

Getting there
Metro-North from Grand Central to Cold Spring, then a pre-booked taxi. Roughly two hours overall is a planning estimate; the group-camp entrance and last-mile journey need confirming.
Staying together
The park confirms that its Group Wilderness Campground is open in 2026. Capacity, price, toilets, water, and cooking arrangements need a direct check with the park office: 845-225-7207.
Timing
The regular family campground is closed for the whole 2026 season for construction. This is a separate group-camping inquiry, not a proposal to book five family sites.
To work through
Confirm group eligibility, seasonal dates, facilities, the location’s distance from construction, and a suitable common space. Promising, but not yet a fully checked venue.
Explore Fahnestock ↗

Catskills · NYS DEC campground

North-South Lake

Lakeside camp, forest trails, and long views.

A strong option if we want the camping itself to be central: cooking outside, walking from camp, and spending two nights in the Catskills.

Getting there
Amtrak from Penn to Hudson, then a pre-booked car for roughly 35–40 minutes. Allow about 3 hours from Penn with a coordinated pickup. This is a longer last-mile transfer than the Harriman options.
Staying together
Tent sites, shared toilets and hot showers. A small group site is listed; our final numbers may require adjacent sites. Picnic pavilions can be reserved separately.
Timing
The published 2026 season includes camping through October 24. Suitable spring dates depend on the campground opening.
To work through
Arrange the return car service in advance, secure sites close together, and plan for cold or wet conditions.
Explore North-South Lake ↗

Montauk · New York State Park

Hither Hills

Ocean air, open sky, and time on the beach.

A different kind of retreat setting: beach walks, open horizons, and a campsite near the Atlantic. Most appealing if the group is happy with a longer journey.

Getting there
LIRR from Penn to Montauk, with transfers depending on the train, then roughly 10–15 minutes by taxi. Allow around 3½–4 hours overall, beyond the original 2–3 hour target.
Staying together
Tent camping with shared shower and toilet facilities. Group arrangements are handled by the park; adjacent standard sites are another possibility.
Timing
The overall 2026 camping season runs to November 22, with individual loops closing earlier. Dates and specific sites need confirming.
To work through
Coastal wind and rain, the longer rail journey, and a place for the whole group to gather. Swimming depends on the season and park rules.
Explore Hither Hills ↗

These are examples, not confirmed bookings. Travel times are planning estimates from a Manhattan rail terminal and assume a coordinated onward transfer. We will confirm dates, group space, facilities, and transport before asking anyone to commit. Park information reviewed September 2026.

Choices we can make together

Shape it around
the people coming.

This invitation shows one version of the retreat. The cohort, learning focus, pace, and length can all be tailored with input from participants, partners, and faculty.

The constant: time to know each other, reflect, practice something useful, and support one another. We would choose a small number of priorities for each group.

01 · Career stage

Who is this moment for?

An early-career group might explore direction, confidence, and finding its voice. A mid-career group might work on influence, difficult trade-offs, or sustaining its commitment. A mixed group could create useful mentoring relationships.

This draft: early- and mid-career sustainability practitioners.

02 · Cohort mix

Who should learn together?

Peers across organizations; people working on a shared challenge; or founders and funders brought together with an accelerator. The mix should serve a clear purpose.

For founders and funders, agree how to handle fundraising relationships and make room for confidential peer-only conversations.

03 · One organization or many

Could this run for a single company?

The draft mixes people from different organizations, which makes candor easier. The same shape can run for one company’s sustainability team or a rising-leader cohort: a shared context, live cases drawn from the same organization, and a link back to the business afterward. Questions to settle: who sponsors it, whether managers attend with their teams, and what leaves the room.

For a single organization, we would design with the sponsor and treat the retreat as the start of an internal peer group.

04 · Learning focus

What would help this group?

The current draft practices a difficult conversation involving conflict or influence. Another version could center on a values compass, inspired by FLITE: clarifying what matters and how it guides choices. Other options include listening, feedback, or navigating uncertainty.

Choose one central practice for two nights. We do not need to cover the whole list.

05 · Pace and activity

How much should we do?

More walking, outdoor challenges, and debriefs; or more quiet reflection, unstructured conversation, and rest. Agree the physical demands and offer ways to participate without taking a long hike.

This draft: two central sessions, shared cooking, and protected open time.

06 · Time away

Would another day change it?

Friday to Sunday keeps the time commitment smaller. Starting Thursday evening adds a full day for a longer hike, solo reflection, and less hurried conversations, if the cohort can make the time.

An extra day creates space; it need not mean another day of workshops. Both lengths are costed in Admin & costs.

07 · Faculty and guests

Whose experience would help?

Choose faculty around the learning focus. A guest practitioner, founder, investor, or leader could join a fireside about careers and turning points. The value would be in candid stories and questions.

No outside speaker is confirmed. Any additional guest arrangements would be reflected in the final price.

08 · Setting and access

What helps everyone settle in?

Tents or cabins, shared or individual sleeping arrangements, access to showers, accessible paths, dietary needs, and a workable wet-weather plan. These choices affect who can comfortably come.

No camping experience required. Agree the arrangements before anyone commits.

09 · Group size and funding

How small, and who pays?

A smaller group gives each person more space; a larger group spreads fixed costs. We are exploring 12–18 participants; the cost table in Admin & costs shows what the size does to the price. Employer or partner support could make participation possible for people paying personally.

Agree sponsorship and confidentiality boundaries so funding does not determine what people feel able to say.

10 · Before and after

How far should it extend?

A short reflection before arriving; a peer partner or small pod afterward; one reunion or a longer sequence. We can tailor the follow-through to what the group will actually use.

This draft: light preparation, a peer check-in within a month, and a proposed reunion around six weeks later.

What would you change?

Tell us who you would bring together, the one thing you would want them to work on, and whether an extra day would be possible. Those answers will help us shape the next version.

The practical details

Who, what,
and what comes next.

This is a draft invitation. We are testing interest and shaping the retreat before confirming the dates, site, and cost.

Who is behind it

A Planetary PS × Treeline Development collaboration

We are designing and running this together: sustainability practice and the peer network from Planetary PS, retreat design and outdoor facilitation from Treeline Development. The two of us are the faculty; the cohort and its partners shape the rest.

Dee Yang

Former McKinsey partner and head of the Systemiq US office

The FLITE and LEAD courses Dee taught at McKinsey are part of the inspiration for this retreat: time for reflection, learning with peers, and practice grounded in real experience.

Alexander “Zander” Martin

Principal, Treeline Development
Senior Faculty, NOLS

Zander brings twenty years of experience in facilitation, coaching, and consulting, designing leadership development experiences and helping teams work well together. His work has included NASA mission crews, fighter squadrons, MBA students, and business leaders.

A former professional explorer who circumnavigated the Earth by ski, foot, canoe, and bicycle, he holds a master’s from Harvard in Leadership Development and Organizational Behavior.

What it costs

Indicative all-in budget · USD

About $1,650 to $2,250 per person

For Friday to Sunday with two faculty: about $2,250 per person at 12 participants, falling to about $1,650 at 18. A Thursday-evening start adds a night and a full day, and about $400 per person at 18.

Included in the estimate: round-trip rail travel from Manhattan and shared station transfers; campsite reservations; meals, snacks, and nonalcoholic drinks; a basic shared-tent and sleeping-kit allowance; program design and facilitation by two faculty, budgeted at a day rate for each day on site; planning, supplies, and a 10 percent contingency.

On price: pricing per participant would be adjusted down based on the faculty day rate. For the first cohort we would aim for roughly $800 per person.

These are rounded planning estimates for a simple Hudson Valley group-camping retreat, not a confirmed price or a quote for every venue listed. Final dates, site, equipment needs, and faculty arrangements will determine the amount. Travel to Manhattan, cabin upgrades, or additional paid guests would need a revised package.

What we ask of you

  • Come for the whole weekend and leave the laptop behind.
  • Do a short reflection before you arrive.
  • Bring one real situation from work you are willing to discuss, without sharing confidential employer information.
  • Help with camp, cooking, and clearing up.
  • Keep personal stories within the group, and respect everyone’s choice about what to share.
